worksheet.title: Start and Go
worksheet.subtitle: Run the blocks to find Bit's number
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read a code and find the number Bit lands on.

parts.title: Read the code
parts.text: Bit moves on a number path. The green start block tells Bit which number to begin on. Each blue forward block moves Bit that many steps along the path. Run the blocks from the TOP, one at a time, to find the number Bit lands on.

parts.title: Run Code A
parts.prompt: Start on 0. Run each block in order: forward 2, then forward 1. What number does Bit land on? Write the number.

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: PREDICT first: what number will Bit land on? Write your guess. Then run Code B from 1 and check. Were you right?

parts.title: You try — change a block
parts.prompt: In Code B, change forward 3 to forward 2. Predict the new landing number, then run it to check. What number now?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Code is a list of blocks that run in order from the top. The start block goes first to set Bit's number, then each move block runs one at a time.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read a short block program and run it on a number path to find where Bit lands, then alter one block and predict the new result. This is the reading-and-running half of coding (C3.1) plus a first taste of altering code and describing the effect (C3.2).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-6 (tape and number cards) so a child can walk each program.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run Code A aloud — 'start at 0… forward 2 lands on 2… forward 1 lands on 3.' One step per block, top to bottom.
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — students run Code A to 3. Exercise 2 — predict Code B's landing (4), then run from 1 to confirm.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — change forward 3 to forward 2; predict and run to land on 3.
4. Connect: 'Code runs in order from the top. The start block must go first so Bit knows where to begin.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Code A: 0 → (forward 2) 2 → (forward 1) 3. Bit lands on 3.
Ex 2 — Code B: 1 → (forward 3) 4. Bit lands on 4.
Ex 3 — change to forward 2: 1 → 3. Bit lands on 3.

Why the order works: the start block runs first to set Bit's number; if a move block ran before the start, Bit would have no number to move from and the code would break. The moves then run top to bottom, one at a time.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: counting the start number as the first step — 'start at 0' is a position, not a move; the first forward step leaves 0.
Simplify: walk each program on a floor number path, pausing on each number.
Extend: ask students to change the start block to 'start at 2' and predict Code A's new landing (5).
Success indicator: the child runs the blocks in order and writes the correct landing number for each code.
